title: Revalidation

description: How Cloudflare revalidates stale cached content with your origin.

Cloudflare revalidates cached content with your origin after the content expires. To revalidate cached content before it expires, [invalidate it](/cache/guides/invalidate-cache/).

## Stale-while-revalidate

When a cached asset expires, Cloudflare uses the [`stale-while-revalidate`](/cache/concepts/cache-control/#revalidation) directive in `Cache-Control` to determine whether it can continue serving the stale asset while fetching a fresh copy from the origin. If the directive is present and the asset is within the allowed staleness window, Cloudflare serves the expired content to visitors and revalidates in the background. By using headers like `If-Modified-Since` and `ETag`, Cloudflare validates content without fully re-fetching it, reducing origin traffic.

## Asynchronous revalidation

Revalidation is fully asynchronous. When a cached asset expires and `stale-while-revalidate` is set, the first request that arrives after expiry triggers revalidation in the background. That request immediately receives stale content with an [UPDATING](/cache/concepts/cache-responses/#updating) status instead of blocking until the origin responds. All following requests also receive stale content with an `UPDATING` status until the origin responds. Once revalidation completes, subsequent requests receive fresh content with a [HIT](/cache/concepts/cache-responses/#hit) status.

If the stale content is still valid, your origin answers `304 Not Modified` and Cloudflare sets a new TTL. If the content has changed, your origin sends the new content with a new `ETag`, or a later `Last-Modified` if it sends no `ETag`, and it replaces the old content. For the rules your origin must follow, refer to [Origin requirements for revalidation](#origin-requirements-for-revalidation).

## Origin requirements for revalidation

To revalidate, Cloudflare sends your origin a conditional request. `If-None-Match` carries the cached `ETag`, and `If-Modified-Since` carries the cached `Last-Modified`. Your origin must follow the HTTP rules for conditional requests:

- **Answer a matching `If-None-Match` with `304`.** On a `GET` or `HEAD` request, if an entity tag listed in `If-None-Match` matches the `ETag` of the response your origin would send, respond with `304 Not Modified`, not `200` ([RFC 9110, section 13.1.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.2)). Compare entity tags with the weak comparison function, which ignores the `W/` prefix ([RFC 9110, section 8.8.3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.3.2)).
- **Change the `ETag` whenever the content changes.** Responses that share an `ETag` are interchangeable as far as caches are concerned. A strong `ETag` changes whenever the response body changes, by definition. A weak `ETag` ought to change whenever you want caches to stop using old responses ([RFC 9110, section 8.8.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.1)).
- **Keep `Last-Modified` accurate.** It is the time the content last changed ([RFC 9110, section 8.8.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.2)). When a `GET` or `HEAD` request carries `If-Modified-Since` without `If-None-Match`, answer `304` if the content has not changed since that time. When the request carries both, ignore `If-Modified-Since` and let `If-None-Match` decide ([RFC 9110, section 13.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.3)).

A `200` response that repeats the cached `ETag` tells every cache that the old and new content are interchangeable, even if its `Last-Modified` is later, so the new content does not reliably replace the old content. With [Tiered Cache](/cache/how-to/tiered-cache/), a lower-tier data center revalidates its copy with its upper-tier data center. The upper tier receives the new content from your origin, but its `ETag` matches the lower tier's copy, so the upper tier answers the lower tier with `304` and the lower tier keeps serving the old content. Browsers that cached the old response revalidate the same way and keep their copy too. This applies whether the content expired or was [invalidated](/cache/guides/invalidate-cache/).

## Controlling stale behavior

Cloudflare only serves stale content during revalidation if your origin includes the `stale-while-revalidate` directive in its `Cache-Control` header. Without this directive, visitors wait for the origin to respond before receiving content.

If your origin sets `stale-while-revalidate` but you want to override it, you can disable stale serving through the [Serve stale content while revalidating](/cache/how-to/cache-rules/settings/#serve-stale-content-while-revalidating) setting in Cache Rules.

### Directives that disable stale-while-revalidate

When [Origin Cache Control](/cache/concepts/cache-control/#enable-origin-cache-control) is enabled, the following `Cache-Control` directives prevent Cloudflare from serving stale content, per [RFC 9111 §4.2.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-4.2.4):

- **`must-revalidate`** — Prohibits serving stale content; the cache must revalidate with the origin first.
- **`proxy-revalidate`** — Same as `must-revalidate`, but only applies to shared caches (like Cloudflare).
- **`s-maxage`** — Implies `proxy-revalidate` semantics, so shared caches cannot serve stale content.
- **`no-cache`** — Requires revalidation before serving any cached response.

If any of these directives are present alongside `stale-while-revalidate`, Cloudflare will not serve stale content — requests will return `EXPIRED` instead of `UPDATING`.

:::note[Workaround for different edge and browser TTLs]
If you need `stale-while-revalidate` behavior with a different TTL for Cloudflare than for browsers, do not use `s-maxage`. Instead, configure your origin to send `max-age` with `stale-while-revalidate`, then use [Edge Cache TTL](/cache/how-to/cache-rules/settings/#edge-ttl) in Cache Rules to set a separate TTL for Cloudflare.
:::

For all available directives or behavior when Origin Cache Control is disabled, refer to [Cache-Control directives](/cache/concepts/cache-control/#cache-control-directives).

## Smart revalidation towards users

When both [`Last-Modified`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7232?cf_history_state=%7B%22guid%22%3A%22C255D9FF78CD46CDA4F76812EA68C350%22%2C%22historyId%22%3A15%2C%22targetId%22%3A%226C8153BAEF7BC0C5A331E28F8BCF1ABA%22%7D#section-2.2) and [`Etag`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7232?cf_history_state=%7B%22guid%22%3A%22C255D9FF78CD46CDA4F76812EA68C350%22%2C%22historyId%22%3A13%2C%22targetId%22%3A%226C8153BAEF7BC0C5A331E28F8BCF1ABA%22%7D#section-2.3) headers are absent from the origin server response, Smart Edge Revalidation will use the time the object was cached on Cloudflare's global network as the `Last-Modified` header value. When a browser sends a revalidation request to Cloudflare using `If-Modified-Since` or `If-None-Match`, our global network can answer those revalidation questions using the `Last-Modified` header generated from Smart Edge Revalidation. In this way, our global network can ensure efficient revalidation even if the headers are not sent from the origin.
